list.listitem: Although most patients with mild disease are asymptomatic, those with severe disease have significant anemia, jaundice, splenomegaly, and an increased risk of pigment gallstones. B

Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) may be diagnosed on the basis of a positive family history; characteristic findings of pallor, jaundice, and splenomegaly; and typical laboratory features (anemia, reticulocytosis, increased mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration [MCHC], increased red cell distribution width [RDW], and spherocytes). B

Splenectomy is only required in patients with moderate-to-severe disease who require frequent transfusions; postsplenectomy patients have an increased risk of sepsis and should be vaccinated against encapsulated organisms. B
Partial or subtotal splenectomy may be protective against infection. C

background.definition: Hereditary spherocytosis is a relatively common, heterogeneous disorder of the erythrocyte membrane causing hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly. The clinical severity varies widely; the majority of cases are mild to moderate. Although the diagnosis is often made in childhood, hereditary spherocytosis may present later in life.

list.listitem: 1:2000 to 1:5000 in patients of Northern European ancestry
Less frequent among African Americans and those of Southeast Asian ancestry
It is reported to be the most common cause of congenital hemolytic anemia among individuals of Northern European ancestry.
Up to 1% of severely jaundiced neonates have hereditary spherocytosis.
There is a family history of hereditary spherocytosis in approximately 75% of patients with the disorder, reflecting an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.
Some cases may be inherited recessively; this may be more common in patients of non-European ancestry.
Sporadic cases have also been described.
The aplastic crisis of hereditary spherocytosis may be precipitated by any viral infection, most commonly parvovirus.

The molecular defects in hereditary spherocytosis involve the cytoskeleton within the red cell membrane, specifically mutations in proteins responsible for maintaining the vertical attachments of the cytoskeleton to the overlying lipid bilayer.
Defects in ankyrin are the most common (50%-60%).
Other defects are found in spectrin (20%), band 3 (15%-20%), and protein 4.2 (<5%).
The result of these defects is a loss of red blood cell membrane surface area and subsequent transformation of cells from discoid to spherocyte.
With less deformability, spherocytes are unable to traverse the spleen and are removed from circulation, leading to the characteristic anemia.
In patients who require splenectomy, care must be taken to provide immunization against encapsulated organisms. B

For individuals older than 2 years who require splenectomy, vaccination against pneumococcus (using a polysaccharide vaccine) should be given at least 2 weeks prior to surgery, and then every 5 years thereafter. Children who have not received the conjugate pneumococcal vaccine or Haemophilus influenza vaccination should receive these prior to surgery. Vaccination against meningococcus is also recommended at least 2 weeks prior to surgery and every 3 to 5 years thereafter, although there are fewer data supporting an adequate immune response in splenectomized individuals. C
Prior to splenectomy, it is important to rule out hereditary stomatocytosis as there is increased risk of thrombosis in splenectomized individuals with stomatocytosis. C

For individuals with a positive family history of hereditary spherocytosis, the combination of clinical signs and symptoms (anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly) and characteristic laboratory findings (anemia with spherocytes, increased MCHC, and reticulocytosis) is sufficient to make the diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis. B

In equivocal cases in which further testing is considered necessary, the eosin-5-maleimide (EMA) binding test has a high predictive value, especially when used in conjunction with other supporting evidence (high MCHC, reticulocytosis, anemia, and jaundice). Cryohemolysis test also appears to have high predictive value in confirming the diagnosis, though it can produce false positives in the setting of iron deficiency anemia.B
An osmotic fragility test, formerly considered to be the gold standard, may be useful in confirming the diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis, but it has relatively low sensitivity and specificity. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Positive direct antiglobulin test; no significant family history
Low reticulocyte count; binucleate erythroblasts on bone marrow testing

list.listitem: Hereditary spherocytosis is characterized clinically by anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly.
In 75% of cases, there is a family history of hereditary spherocytosis, splenomegaly, or splenectomy.
Suspect hereditary spherocytosis in a significantly jaundiced neonate; several recent studies have suggested that the prevalence of hereditary spherocytosis may be as high as 1% in this population.
Pigment gallstones may be seen in up to 60% of patients, usually among those 10 years or older.
In clinically suspicious cases with a positive family history for hereditary spherocytosis, the presence of anemia with spherocytes and reticulocytes is adequate for diagnosis.

The clinical presentation is generally classified as mild, moderate, or severe on the basis of laboratory results. Mild cases may escape diagnosis for years and be identified only by laboratory findings of anemia and spherocytes, or after an aplastic crisis associated with Parvovirus B19 infection. Moderate cases are characterized by a hemoglobin level of 8 to 12 g/dL and a reticulocyte count greater than 6%. In severe cases, there is significant anemia with a hemoglobin level of 6 to 8 g/dL and a reticulocyte count greater than 10%.
In a group of neonates with hyperbilirubinemia, an MCHC of greater than 36 had a sensitivity of 82% and a specificity of 98% for the diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis.

The osmotic fragility test has been used to confirm the diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis. However, the test is difficult to perform, is labor intensive, and false-positive results may be seen in patients with other hemolytic anemias, renal failure, pregnancy, and in those with an elevated reticulocyte count. In 1 series of 300 patients, the sensitivity of this test ranged from 48% to 95% and was independent of the type and degree of the red blood cell membrane defect.

The EMA test, a fluorscein-based flow cytometry assay, which can be performed in as little as 2 hours has been described as having a sensitivity as high as 96% and a specificity of 99.1% for hereditary spherocytosis.

The cryohemolysis test (incubation of erythrocytes in hypertonic solution, with cooling) can be used in screening for HS, though there is still inter-laboratory variability and results are not pathognomonic for HS.
Sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) can be used to confirm erythrocyte protein abnormalities; however, this assay is not easily available or routinely performed.
Ultrasound of the gall bladder is recommended to look for cholelithiasis every 3 to 5 years after the age of 10 years.

Patients typically present with hemolytic anemia, jaundice, and splenomegaly; reticulocytosis and spherocytes may also be seen on peripheral blood smear. It is important to remember that spherocytes can also be seen in autoimmune hemolytic anemia and other disorders.

In most patients, hereditary spherocytosis may be diagnosed on the basis of a positive family history, along with the characteristic physical examination findings of pallor, jaundice, and splenomegaly, and laboratory features (anemia, reticulocytosis, increased MCHC, increased RDW, and spherocytes).
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to evaluation.
For mild cases, splenectomy is not indicated; for moderate-to-severe cases, splenectomy may be indicated depending upon the need for transfusion, subsequent hemosiderosis, and the degree of anemia. B
Splenectomy should not be performed before the age of 6 years, except in very severe cases. B
There is strong evidence to suggest benefit of laparoscopic over traditional splenectomy, and of near-total splenectomy over total splenectomy. B

For all individuals considering splenectomy, and for all who have had the procedure, immunization against encapsulated organisms is essential. The risk of sepsis due to encapsulated organisms must be explained prior to the procedure. B
Folate may be beneficial in cases of moderate or severe disease. There is no strong evidence to support a recommended dose, but common regimens vary from 2 mg per day to 5 mg per day.

Daily oral penicillin V is recommended after splenectomy because of the lifelong risk for sepsis; however, the optimal duration of treatment is undetermined. This recommendation was based on studies conducted prior to the use of PCV-7 vaccine in patients with sickle cell disease. Additionally, increased penicillin resistance of pneumococcal strains necessitates attention to local resistance patterns.
Splenectomy may be recommended in patients with severe anemia requiring multiple transfusions; this usually results in a marked amelioration of symptoms, although mild hemolysis may persist.

Splenectomy should be delayed, if possible, until the age of 6 years. The diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis must be confirmed prior to splenectomy, as splenectomy should be avoided in individuals with hereditary stomatocytosis because of the increased risk of thrombotic complications.

There is a lifetime risk of increased infections with encapsulated organisms following splenectomy and a potential increased risk of thrombotic events and pulmonary hypertension. These risks must be balanced with the potential benefits. However there is not enough evidence to support the use of prophylactic anticoagulation following splenectomy.

There is some evidence to suggest that near-total or partial splenectomy may provide some immunologic benefit over total splenectomy. However, recurrent hemolysis, remnant regrowth, and the need for secondary operations are more likely with this procedure.

A meta-analysis identified 5 retrospective cohort studies comparing partial with total splenectomy. Outcomes were generally similar, with a higher risk of post-operative cholelithiasis with partial surgery.

Laparoscopic splenectomy has gained favor over traditional laparotomy; benefits may include shorter hospital stay and fewer surgical complications. However, results of one retrospective study suggested that laparoscopic partial splenectomy was associated with more pain, longer time to oral intake, and longer hospital stay. The study design means the level of evidence is very low.
Cholecystectomy should be performed for those with cholelithiasis; prophylactic cholecystectomy is not warranted.
Transfusions may be necessary in severe cases and during an aplastic crisis.
Vaccines against encapsulated organisms (eg, pneumococcus, meningococcus, H. influenza) should be administered at least 2 weeks prior to splenectomy and every 3 to 5 years thereafter.
Patients with aplastic crisis or those requiring transfusions should be hospitalized and referred to (or managed in consultation with) a hematologist.
The majority of patients with mild disease are asymptomatic; those with moderate-to-severe disease may require splenectomy, which significantly decreases hemolysis and the need for transfusions. B

Aplastic crisis may be precipitated by any viral infection; parvovirus B19 may cause significant anemia, in some cases necessitating blood transfusion. Complete recovery usually occurs within 10 to 14 days. B
Postsplenectomy complications include the risk of sepsis, thrombosis and pulmonary hypertension. B
There is no indication for physical activity restriction despite the presence of enlarged spleens in these patients. B
Anemia may worsen during pregnancy secondary to increased plasma volume and hemodilution, but usually this does not require any additional intervention.
Splenectomy should be delayed, if possible, until the age of 6 years.
